summary: Defines the manifest for the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI): a signed file listing all the signed objects at a publication point in an RPKI repository. This lets relying parties check that they have everything an authority has published. It obsoletes RFC 6486. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A manifest is like a packing slip in a box. It lists everything that should be inside, so if something is missing or swapped, the receiver can tell.

questions: how do relying parties detect missing rpki objects
what is a one-time-use ee certificate
what happens when an rpki fetch fails
subtitle: A signed packing list that lets RPKI validators notice when files at a repository have been removed, swapped for stale copies or tampered with.

tldr.problem: Every RPKI object is digitally signed, but signatures alone cannot reveal that a stale (superseded but unexpired) object was substituted, or that an object was removed in flight.
tldr.mechanism: Each CA publishes a signed manifest listing the file name and hash of every object at its publication point. A relying party fetches the manifest, checks it is current, and checks that every listed file is present and matches its hash.
tldr.outcome: If anything is missing, stale or mismatched, the fetch counts as failed and the relying party keeps using its cached copies. This document obsoletes RFC 6486 and has since been updated by RFC 9981.

today: RFC 9286 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022. It obsoletes RFC 6486 and has been updated by RFC 9981.

sections.title: Why Signatures Are Not Enough
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) stores signed objects in a distributed repository system. Because each object is signed by whoever created it, anyone can detect an attack that modifies an object. Signatures do not help against two other attacks: substituting a stale object (one that was valid and has not expired, but has since been superseded), or removing an object that should be there.

A manifest closes that gap. It is a signed object listing every signed object at a repository publication point, with the file name and a hash of the contents of each file. Manifests are meant to be used at Certification Authority (CA) publication points, which hold subordinate certificates, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) and other signed objects verified by End-Entity (EE) certificates issued by that CA.

Manifests are modeled on CRLs, because detecting stale manifests and replays raises similar issues. This document obsoletes RFC 6486.
sections.eli5: A signature proves who wrote a note, but not that the note is the newest one or that nobody took a note out of the pile. The manifest is a checklist of the whole pile.

sections.title: What a Manifest Covers
sections.content:
A manifest for a CA's publication point lists the non-expired, non-revoked certificates issued and published by that CA, the most recent CRL issued by that CA, and all published signed objects that are verifiable using EE certificates issued by that CA. The manifest does not list itself, because its hash cannot be computed before it is signed.

Every RPKI signed object carries its EE certificate inside its Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) wrapper, so that certificate does not need to be published separately. When several CA instances share one publication point, as can happen during a key rollover, there are several manifests, and each describes only its own CA instance's products.
sections.eli5: The checklist covers every paper that one office has filed in the shared cabinet. If two offices share a cabinet, each keeps its own checklist.

sections.title: The Manifest Structure
sections.content:
A manifest is an RPKI signed object whose eContentType is id-ct-rpkiManifest, with the numerical OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.26. Its content is encoded in ASN.1 using the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) and has six fields.

  • version MUST be 0.
  • manifestNumber is incremented by 1 each time a new manifest is issued. Verifiers MUST handle values up to 20 octets and issuers MUST NOT use longer ones.
  • thisUpdate is when the manifest was created and nextUpdate is when the next one will be issued. The second MUST be later than the first.
  • fileHashAlg is the OID of the hash algorithm, which MUST conform to RFC 7935.
  • fileList is a sequence of FileAndHash entries, each holding a file name and a hash of that file's contents.

File names MUST be one or more characters from a-z, A-Z, 0-9, hyphen or underscore, then a single dot, then a three-letter extension listed in the IANA "RPKI Repository Name Schemes" registry. CAs and RPs MUST be able to handle file names in a case-sensitive, case-preserving way.
sections.eli5: Each manifest has a number that goes up every time, a start time, an expiry time, the name of the fingerprint method used, and a list of file names, each with its fingerprint.

sections.title: How a CA Generates a Manifest
sections.content:
The manifest is signed with a one-time-use EE certificate: the CA MUST sign only one manifest with each generated private key and MUST generate a new key pair for each new version. The steps are:

  1. Generate a new key pair.
  2. Issue an EE certificate for it, with an SIA entry using the id-ad-signedObject access method and the "inherit" attribute for its Internet Number Resources. Its validity interval MUST exactly match thisUpdate to nextUpdate. The CA MUST revoke the EE certificate of the manifest being replaced.
  3. Do not publish the EE certificate at the publication point.
  4. Build the manifest content, listing the file name and hash pair for each object the CA published there.
  5. Sign it with the new private key and publish it.
  6. Destroy the private key.

A new manifest MUST be issued and published before nextUpdate, and whenever objects at the publication point change. The manifest's object URL stays the same across cycles, and repository operators MUST avoid exposing relying parties to inconsistent intermediate states during updates.
sections.eli5: Each time the office updates the checklist, it uses a brand new stamp that works once, then destroys it, so an old checklist can never be re-stamped.

sections.title: How Relying Parties Check a Manifest
sections.content:
A relying party (RP) MUST use the current manifest to decide which files it accepts for validating certificates, ROAs and CRLs. Files not listed MUST NOT be used for that. The RP fetches the manifest named in the CA certificate's SIA and runs these checks in order.

  • Validity: the content type and version are correct and thisUpdate precedes nextUpdate. An invalid manifest is discarded as if none existed.
  • Freshness: the current time must lie between thisUpdate and nextUpdate. Earlier means a possible error, later means the manifest is stale. Either is a failed fetch. The RP also checks that manifestNumber and thisUpdate are higher than for earlier validated manifests.
  • Completeness: every listed file MUST be retrievable from the publication point.
  • Integrity: the hash of each retrieved file MUST match the hash in the manifest.

If any step fails, the RP MUST issue a warning, and it is RECOMMENDED that a human operator be notified. The RP SHOULD keep using cached versions of the objects until they become stale or a later fetch succeeds, and MUST NOT try to validate subordinate objects in the meantime.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks that the checklist is not out of date, that every item on it arrived, and that each item looks exactly right. If not, the receiver keeps using what it already had.

sections.title: What Manifests Protect, and What They Do Not
sections.content:
Manifests help an RP tell whether an object was deleted, hidden or replaced by an older version, even when it fetched the repository over an insecure channel. When the manifest and the fetched contents differ, it can help show which objects are missing, extraneous or superseded.

They cannot repair that damage. Attacks on the manifest itself are detectable within the regular schedule of manifest updates, but replay attacks within finer-grained time frames are not necessarily detectable by the manifest structure.

Because the RP only learns of a problem when it fetches, the manifest's nextUpdate sets the window in which tampering is guaranteed to show up.
sections.eli5: The checklist can tell you something is missing, but it cannot bring the missing thing back. And a swap that happens within the checklist's own lifetime might slip by.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 6486
sections.content:
The document says that in 2019 it came to light that multiple RP implementations were in a vulnerable position, possibly because of perceived ambiguity in RFC 6486. This revision clarifies the specification in light of deployment experience. The listed changes include:

  • Forbidding "sequential-use" EE certificates and mandating "one-time-use" ones.
  • Requiring the EE certificate validity to coincide with the manifest's thisUpdate and nextUpdate.
  • Clarifying that manifestNumber increases in steps of 1.
  • Recommending that the manifest's nextUpdate match the CRL's.
  • Constraining the characters allowed in file names.
  • Clarifying that an RP unable to obtain every listed file is in a failure state and should use cached data if available.
  • Clarifying that a current CRL must be present, listed and verified.
  • Removing the notion of "local policy".
sections.eli5: The rules were rewritten more clearly after people read the old ones in different ways. The new version says exactly what to do, with fewer loopholes.
